Where it began

Fred Trueman was born on 6 February 1931 in Stainton, near Maltby, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, the middle child of seven in a country family. He was bowling by the age of four, and his teachers at the village school soon spotted the talent.

After leaving school at fourteen he played village cricket for Roche Abbey, and then came under the eye of Cyril Turner, a former Yorkshire player coaching at Sheffield United, who taught him to hold the ball properly and swing it both ways. Yorkshire picked him for his first-class debut against Cambridge University in May 1949. Wisden's report called him a spin bowler, a mistake nobody would make twice.

The player

His Test debut came against India at Headingley in June 1952, and it was quite an entrance. In the second innings India lost four wickets before they had a run on the board, three of them to Trueman. He took 29 wickets in that first series, including 8 for 31 at Old Trafford, which stayed his best Test return.

In all he played 67 Tests between 1952 and 1965 and took 307 wickets at 21.58, with 17 five-wicket hauls and three ten-wicket matches. He was the first bowler anywhere to reach 300 Test wickets. For six years from 1957 he shared the new ball with Brian Statham, the steady, accurate partner to his fire, and the two made one of the great opening pairs in Test history.

What made him special

Genuine pace, rhythm and a love of fast bowling. Bill Bowes, one of his early coaches, said he had the three things a fast bowler needs: that love, a powerful build and a smooth cartwheel action. He was also a superb fielder, especially at leg slip, where he once held 36 catches in a season.

His batting was more for entertainment than anything else: a Test average of 13.82. But he did make three first-class hundreds, and against New Zealand at the Oval in 1958 he hit 39 not out in twenty minutes, with three sixes.

Away from the middle

During national service in the RAF he turned out at football for Lincoln City's reserves, and was good enough to be offered professional terms, which he turned down to concentrate on cricket. After he finished playing he became an author and a well-known, outspoken voice on the BBC's Test Match Special.

He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1953, appointed OBE in 1989 and given a place in the ICC Hall of Fame in 2009. In 2018, when England played their 1000th Test, he was picked in the country's greatest Test XI.

And finally

Harold Wilson, the Prime Minister and a Yorkshireman himself, once called him, half in jest, the greatest living Yorkshireman. Fred never seemed inclined to argue.
